President Reagan acted wholly without historical precedent. His moratorium 
was the regulatory analogue of President Jefferson s instruction to Madison to 
hold up the appointments of Marbury and other Federahst judges.) Any 
outgoing president, especially one who is aware that his successor belongs to a 
different pohtical party, will seek in the concluding months of the outgoing 
Administration to put as many regulatory projects into final form as possible. 
This will entrench, at least temporarily, the pohcy preferences of the outgoing 
White House—^precisely the phenomenon President Reagan sought to undo.
President Reagan’s regulatory postponement memo simply directed each 
cabinet agency, including EPA to “postpone for 60 days from the date of this 
memorandum the effective date of all regulations that your agency has 
promulgated in final form and that are scheduled to become effective during 
such 60-day period.” Comparable memos from succeeding Administrations 
paid closer attention to the different categories into which the prior 
Adm 1 m‘stration’s final rulemaking output would faU:
A. 
Rules in final form that have not yet been sent to the Federal 
Register;
B. Final rules sent to the Federal Register, but not yet published;
C. 
Rules published in the Federal Register, but not yet past their 
effective date; and
D. Rules published in the Federal Register and fully in effect.
Typically, these memos would order agencies not to forward to the Federal 
Register any rules in category A until reviewed by the new Administration, to 
withdraw from pubheation (to the extent legally permissible) rules in category 
B, and either to extend for 60 days or to consider extending for 60 days rules 
in Category C. Memos from the George H.W. Bush through Obama 
Administration are collected as an appendix to Jack M. Beermann, Midnight 
Rules: A Reform Agenda (ACUS, 2012). For yet more recent Administrations, 
see Memorandum for the Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies from 
Reince Priebus, Assistant to the President and Chief of Staff re: Regulatory 
Freeze Pending Review, 82 Fed. Reg. 8346 (2017), and Memorandum for the 
Heads of Executive Departments and Agencies from Ronald A. Klain, Assistant 
to the President and Chief of Staff re: Regulatory Freeze Pending Review, 86 
Fed. Reg. 7424 (2021).
A number of Trump Administration agency heads also tried to find 
expeditious ways of delaying or withdrawing Obama Administration 
regulations in Category D. If not effected through a subsequent notice-and- 
comment rulemaking, these efforts were frequently rebuffed in the courts. See, 
e.g.. Clean, Air Courbcil v. Pruitt^ 862 F.3d 1 (D.C. Cir. 2017); Courtcil of Parent
